title: LoRA and Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT)
summary: Full fine-tuning of large models needs enormous GPU memory. LoRA solves this by freezing the base model and training tiny 'adapter' matrices, cutting trainable parameters by over 99%. QLoRA adds quantization so you can fine-tune billion-parameter mod
content:
# LoRA and Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) ##### The 80 GB problem and the 6 GB solution A two-person team in Indore wanted to fine-tune Llama-2-7B on their legal document dataset. They did the memory arithmetic before renting a GPU: ``` Model weights (7B × 2 bytes, fp16) = 14 GB Gradients (7B × 2 bytes) = 14 GB Adam optimiser state (7B × 8 bytes) = 56 GB Activations (batch 4, seq 512) ≈ 4 GB ───────────────────────────────────────────────── Total ≈ 88 GB ``` An A100 has 80 GB. They needed at least two, at roughly ₹250 per hour each on Indian cloud providers. For a project that might not work. They used QLoRA instead. Same model, same dataset, **6.2 GB of VRAM** — a free Google Colab T4. Training took four hours. The result was good enough to ship. The arithmetic above is why parameter-efficient fine-tuning exists, and understanding those four lines is understanding the whole motivation. **Optimiser state is the killer** — Adam stores two 32-bit values per parameter, which is four times the model itself in fp16. LoRA's insight is that you do not need gradients or optimiser state for weights you are not training. ##### Why full fine-tuning is so expensive Break down that 88 GB by what each part is for: | Component | Size for 7B (fp16) | Needed if frozen? | |---|---|---| | Model weights | 14 GB | **Yes** (forward pass) | | Gradients | 14 GB | No | | Adam momentum (m) | 28 GB | No | | Adam variance (v) | 28 GB | No | | Activations | ~4 GB | Reduced | Freeze the base model and three of those five disappear. You still need the weights in memory to run the forward pass, but you need gradients and optimiser state only for the parameters you actually train. If those trainable parameters are 0.1% of the total, your optimiser state drops from 56 GB to 56 MB. The remaining question is: can 0.1% of the parameters carry enough capacity to adapt a model? LoRA's answer is yes, and the reason is interesting. ##### The LoRA idea Hu et al. (2021) started from an empirical observation: **the weight *updates* learned during fine-tuning have low intrinsic rank.** The change $\Delta W$ that fine-tuning applies is much simpler than a full-rank matrix — it lives in a low-dimensional subspace. So instead of learning $\Delta W$ directly (a $d \times k$ matrix), factorise it: $$W' = W_0 + \Delta W = W_0 + BA$$ where $B$ is $d \times r$, $A$ is $r \times k$, and $r \ll \min(d, k)$. ```mermaid flowchart LR X["input x"] --> W0["Frozen W₀
d × k
e.g. 4096 × 4096
16.8M params"] X --> A["A (trainable)
r × k
8 × 4096
32K params"] A --> B["B (trainable)
d × r
4096 × 8
32K params"] W0 --> ADD["+"] B --> SCALE["× α/r"] SCALE --> ADD ADD --> Y["output h"] ``` The numbers in that diagram are the whole argument. A 4096×4096 attention projection has 16.8 million parameters. With rank 8, the two LoRA matrices have 65,536 — **0.39% of the original.** ```python import torch import torch.nn as nn class LoRALinear(nn.Module): """A frozen Linear layer with a trainable low-rank adapter.""" def __init__(self, base_layer: nn.Linear, r=8, alpha=16, dropout=0.05): super().__init__() self.base = base_layer for p in self.base.parameters(): p.requires_grad = False # freeze in_f, out_f = base_layer.in_features, base_layer.out_features self.lora_A = nn.Linear(in_f, r, bias=False) self.lora_B = nn.Linear(r, out_f, bias=False) self.scaling = alpha / r self.dropout = nn.Dropout(dropout) # A gets small random init, B gets ZEROS. nn.init.kaiming_uniform_(self.lora_A.weight, a=5 ** 0.5) nn.init.zeros_(self.lora_B.weight) def forward(self, x): return self.base(x) + self.lora_B(self.lora_A(self.dropout(x))) * self.scaling ``` **Why `B` is initialised to zeros matters.** At step zero, $BA = 0$, so $W' = W_0$ exactly — the adapted model is byte-for-byte identical to the base model. Training starts from the pretrained behaviour rather than from a random perturbation of it. If both matrices were randomly initialised, the first forward pass would inject noise into every layer and you would lose the pretrained knowledge before learning anything. **The hyperparameters:** - **`r` (rank)** — capacity. 8 or 16 for style and format adaptation; 32–64 for learning a genuinely new task. Higher is not automatically better and increases overfitting risk. - **`alpha`** — scaling. The convention is `alpha = 2r`. Effective learning rate for the adapter scales with `alpha/r`. - **`target_modules`** — which layers get adapters. The original paper used only query and value projections; current practice targets all attention and often the MLP projections too, which usually works better. ##### Using the PEFT library ```python import torch from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model, TaskType MODEL = "meta-llama/Llama-2-7b-hf" model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( MODEL, torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map="auto" ) tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL) tokenizer.pad_token = tokenizer.eos_token lora_config = LoraConfig( task_type=TaskType.CAUSAL_LM, r=16, lora_alpha=32, lora_dropout=0.05, bias="none", target_modules=["q_proj", "k_proj", "v_proj", "o_proj", "gate_proj", "up_proj", "down_proj"], ) model = get_peft_model(model, lora_config) model.print_trainable_parameters() # trainable params: 39,976,960 || all params: 6,778,318,848 || trainable%: 0.5898 ``` **0.59%.** That single line is the whole value proposition. Training proceeds exactly as Day 28 — same `Trainer`, same arguments — with one change: **the learning rate is higher.** LoRA typically uses 1e-4 to 3e-4, roughly 10× full fine-tuning, because the adapter starts from zero and has far fewer parameters to move. ```python from transformers import TrainingArguments, Trainer args = TrainingArguments( output_dir="./llama-legal-lora", learning_rate=2e-4, # ← 10× higher than full FT num_train_epochs=3, per_device_train_batch_size=4, gradient_accumulation_steps=4, warmup_ratio=0.03, lr_scheduler_type="cosine", bf16=True, gradient_checkpointing=True, logging_steps=25, eval_strategy="epoch", save_strategy="epoch", seed=42, ) trainer = Trainer(model=model, args=args, train_dataset=train_ds, eval_dataset=eval_ds, data_collator=collator) trainer.train() model.save_pretrained("./llama-legal-lora/adapter") # ~80 MB, not 14 GB ``` **The adapter is tens of megabytes.** You can email it, version it in Git LFS, publish it to the Hub, and store fifty task-specific adapters in the space one full fine-tune would need. ##### QLoRA QLoRA (Dettmers et al., 2023) adds quantization: load the **frozen base model in 4-bit** while keeping the LoRA adapters in 16-bit. The frozen weights only need to be accurate enough for a good forward pass. They receive no gradients, so quantization error does not compound through training. ```python import torch from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, BitsAndBytesConfig from peft import prepare_model_for_kbit_training, LoraConfig, get_peft_model bnb_config = BitsAndBytesConfig( load_in_4bit=True, bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4", # NormalFloat4 — info-theoretically optimal bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16, # compute in bf16, store in 4-bit bnb_4bit_use_double_quant=True, # quantize the quantization constants too ) model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( "meta-llama/Llama-2-7b-hf", quantization_config=bnb_config, device_map="auto", ) model = prepare_model_for_kbit_training(model, use_gradient_checkpointing=True) model = get_peft_model(model, lora_config) model.print_trainable_parameters() ``` Three techniques stack here: - **NF4** — a 4-bit datatype designed for normally-distributed weights, which neural network weights approximately are. Better fidelity than naive int4. - **Double quantization** — quantizing the quantization constants saves another ~0.4 bits per parameter. - **Paged optimisers** — spill optimiser state to CPU RAM during memory spikes, preventing OOM crashes. The memory result: | Approach | 7B model | 13B | 70B | |---|---|---|---| | Full fine-tune (fp16 + Adam) | ~88 GB | ~160 GB | ~800 GB | | LoRA (fp16 base) | ~18 GB | ~32 GB | ~160 GB | | **QLoRA (4-bit base)** | **~6 GB** | **~10 GB** | **~46 GB** | QLoRA on a 7B model fits in a free Colab T4. That single fact democratised LLM fine-tuning more than any other development. The trade-off is speed: 4-bit dequantization on every forward pass costs roughly 30–40% throughput. Quality loss is small — the QLoRA paper reported matching 16-bit full fine-tuning performance on their benchmarks. ##### Merging adapters For deployment you can fold the adapter back into the base weights, eliminating inference overhead entirely. ```python from peft import PeftModel from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM # Load base in full precision (NOT 4-bit) for merging base = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( "meta-llama/Llama-2-7b-hf", torch_dtype=torch.float16, device_map="cpu" ) model = PeftModel.from_pretrained(base, "./llama-legal-lora/adapter") merged = model.merge_and_unload() # W' = W₀ + BA, computed once merged.save_pretrained("./llama-legal-merged") tokenizer.save_pretrained("./llama-legal-merged") ``` **Merged versus unmerged:** | | Merged | Unmerged | |---|---|---| | Inference latency | Baseline | +5–10% | | Disk | Full model (14 GB) | Adapter only (~80 MB) | | Swap tasks at runtime | No | **Yes** | | Serve N tasks | N full models | 1 base + N adapters | **Do not merge a QLoRA adapter into a 4-bit base.** Load the base in fp16 for the merge, or you compound quantization error. This is a genuinely common mistake. The unmerged path enables something powerful: one base model in GPU memory serving many specialised behaviours by hot-swapping adapters per request. Frameworks like vLLM support this directly, and it is how you offer per-customer fine-tunes economically. ##### Other PEFT methods | Method | Approach | Trainable | Notes | |---|---|---|---| | **LoRA** | Low-rank update matrices | 0.1–1% | **The default** | | **QLoRA** | LoRA + 4-bit base | 0.1–1% | Lowest memory | | **DoRA** | Decomposes magnitude and direction | 0.1–1% | Slightly better than LoRA | | **Prefix tuning** | Trainable vectors prepended to keys/values | ~0.1% | Consumes context length | | **Prompt tuning** | Trainable soft prompt embeddings | <0.1% | Only works well at large scale | | **IA³** | Learned rescaling vectors | ~0.01% | Extremely light | | **Adapters** | Small bottleneck layers inserted | 1–5% | Adds inference latency | **LoRA and QLoRA are what you should use.** The others are worth knowing exist; LoRA won on the combination of quality, simplicity, and the ability to merge away the inference cost. ##### Common mistakes - **Learning rate too low.** LoRA wants 1e-4 to 3e-4, not 2e-5. Using the full-fine-tune rate makes it look like LoRA does not work. - **Rank too high** for a simple task — wasted memory and faster overfitting. - **Targeting only `q_proj` and `v_proj`** because the original paper did. Include all attention and MLP projections. - **Merging a QLoRA adapter into a 4-bit base**, compounding quantization error. - **Forgetting `prepare_model_for_kbit_training`** before applying LoRA to a quantized model. - **Expecting LoRA to teach large amounts of new factual knowledge.** It adapts behaviour; use RAG for facts. - **Not calling `print_trainable_parameters()`** to verify the adapter actually attached. - **Saving the whole model** instead of just the adapter, losing the size advantage. - **Mismatched base model** at load time — the adapter is meaningless against different weights. - **`fp16` instead of `bf16`** on Ampere-or-newer GPUs; bf16 is far more numerically stable for LLM training. - **Assuming QLoRA is free.** It is 30–40% slower per step than plain LoRA. ##### Hands-on: fit a 7B model on a free GPU Your practical task fine-tunes a 7B model with LoRA on a free GPU notebook. Use Colab with a T4, QLoRA config, and a small instruction dataset — `databricks/dolly-15k` sampled down to 1,000 rows works well. Print `print_trainable_parameters()` and note the percentage; watch `nvidia-smi` and note the memory. Those two numbers, roughly 0.6% and roughly 6 GB, are the ones to remember, because they are what you will cite when someone asks whether fine-tuning is affordable. The mini project builds a domain assistant with QLoRA and publishes the adapter to the Hub. Publishing is the part worth doing properly: write a model card covering base model, dataset, hyperparameters, intended use, and limitations — Day 42's governance material applies. An adapter on the Hub with a real model card is a stronger portfolio item than most complete projects, precisely because it is a small artifact that demonstrates you understand the whole pipeline. The assignment compares full fine-tuning against LoRA on memory, speed, and quality. Use a small model — DistilGPT-2 or GPT-2 — so full fine-tuning is actually feasible for the comparison. Measure peak VRAM with `torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated()`, wall-clock time, and evaluation loss plus generation quality on a held-out set. The expected result is that LoRA uses a fraction of the memory for very similar quality, and being able to quote your own numbers rather than the paper's is what makes the write-up credible. ##### Key takeaways - **Optimiser state, not model weights, is what makes full fine-tuning expensive** — Adam needs 8 bytes per parameter, four times the fp16 model itself. - **LoRA freezes the base model and trains low-rank matrices** whose product approximates the weight update, cutting trainable parameters to under 1%. - **Initialising B to zeros means training starts exactly at the pretrained model**, which is why LoRA does not disrupt existing knowledge. - **QLoRA's 4-bit frozen base brings 7B fine-tuning to 6 GB** — a free Colab GPU — at a 30–40% speed cost and minimal quality loss. - **Use lr 1e-4 to 3e-4, target all attention and MLP projections**, and keep adapters unmerged when you need to serve many behaviours from one base model.
